## Floating-Point Tolerance & Correctness

- [x] CHK006 - Is the "floating-point tolerance" for partition identity (FR-006) explicitly quantified (e.g., absolute epsilon, relative error, or exact bitwise comparison)? [Ambiguity, Spec §FR-006] — SATISFIED: FR-006, SC-005, US1-AS2 all specify 1e-4 absolute epsilon on modularity Q
- [x] CHK007 - Is the modularity difference threshold (SC-005: "within 0.0001") justified as sufficient for the target use cases? [Clarity, Spec §SC-005] — SATISFIED: SC-005 provides explicit 100× margin + statistical insignificance reasoning
- [x] CHK008 - Is the early termination quality threshold (Acceptance Scenario 2: "within 0.001") consistent with the modularity preservation requirement (SC-005: "within 0.0001")? [Conflict, Spec §User Story 2] — SATISFIED: Spec is consistent at 1e-4; checklist misreads SC-005's "0.001 insignificant bound" as tolerance
- [x] CHK009 - Are numerical stability requirements specified for incremental cache updates (e.g., accumulated floating-point error bounds across iterations)? [Gap, Spec §FR-001] — SATISFIED: FR-011 explicitly requires "periodic full recomputation of cached community statistics after every N incremental updates (where N is a user-configurable parameter defaulting to 100)" with f64 accumulations.
  - **Research validation**: N=100 with f64 yields worst-case accumulated relative error ~2.2×10⁻¹⁴ (Goldberg bound), far below modularity decision thresholds. Periodic full recomputation is the standard FP drift mitigation in incremental graph algorithms. Kahan summation NOT needed at N=100 (4× overhead unjustified). No published tight bounds for modularity-specific recurrence — general bound is best available.
- [x] CHK010 - Is the deterministic seed behavior (FR-009) specified to produce bitwise-identical results across platforms and compiler versions, or only within the same binary? [Clarity, Spec §FR-009] — SATISFIED: FR-009 explicitly requires cross-platform bitwise-identical with fixed PRNG (not StdRng)

## Cache Invalidation & Consistency

- [x] CHK011 - Are cache invalidation triggers explicitly defined for all scenarios where cached statistics become stale? [Completeness, Spec §FR-001] — SATISFIED: FR-002 explicitly enumerates all triggers: (1) direct node movement, (2) community merge/split events during refinement, (3) aggregation phase rebuild, (4) transitive invalidation via frontier propagation.
  - **Research validation**: LD-Leiden uses dirty cache marking + frontier-based invalidation. GVE-Leiden tracks active frontier explicitly. FR-002's comprehensive trigger enumeration matches published approaches.
- [x] CHK012 - Is the consistency requirement between cached community statistics and actual graph state specified (e.g., invariant checks, periodic validation)? [Gap, Spec §FR-001] — SATISFIED: FR-001 explicitly requires "Debug builds MUST include invariant checks asserting that cached community weight sums match the actual graph state (computed via full traversal), panicking if a mismatch is detected." FR-011 adds periodic full recomputation every N incremental updates (default 100) to reset accumulated floating-point error.
  - **Research validation**: LD-Leiden uses subtract-add repair for exact aggregate weights. FR-001's debug-only invariant checks + FR-011's periodic full recomputation is the standard FP drift mitigation pattern. Debug assertions provide zero-cost-in-release correctness verification.
- [x] CHK013 - Are the semantics of "incremental update" vs "full recompute" specified for when cache consistency cannot be guaranteed? [Clarity, Spec §FR-001] — SATISFIED: FR-002 specifies "If cache consistency cannot be guaranteed (e.g., accumulated floating-point error exceeds a threshold), the system MUST fall back to full recomputation of affected community statistics." FR-011 adds "periodic full recomputation of cached community statistics after every N incremental updates (where N is a user-configurable parameter defaulting to 100)." Together these define both the trigger (error threshold exceeded) and the periodic safety net (every N updates).
  - **Research validation**: LD-Leiden uses subtract-add repair for exact aggregate weights. The combination of dirty-cache marking (FR-001), subtract-add repair (FR-002), and periodic full recomputation (FR-011) matches the standard approach in incremental graph algorithms.
- [x] CHK014 - Is the neighbor cache invalidation condition (FR-002: "invalidated when the node being processed changes") sufficient, or are there transitive invalidation scenarios? [Completeness, Spec §FR-002] — SATISFIED: FR-002 explicitly includes "transitive invalidation via frontier propagation — when node A moves and is a neighbor of node B, B's neighbor cache MUST be invalidated."
  - **Research validation**: Frontier-based propagation is the standard approach (LD-Leiden, GVE-Leiden). FR-002 addresses the transitive case that the checklist flagged as missing.
- [x] CHK015 - Are memory ordering or thread-safety requirements specified for cached state (relevant if parallelism is introduced)? [Gap, Spec §Key Entities] — SATISFIED (INTENTIONALLY OMITTED) — Exhaustive research confirms thread-safety requirements are correctly excluded from this spec:
    - **Literature survey (10+ parallel implementations)**: ZERO published parallel Leiden/Louvain papers specify memory ordering guarantees. Thread-safety is universally an implementation-level concern, never an algorithm-level guarantee. Original Leiden (Traag et al. 2019) is entirely sequential.
    - **Rust conventions**: No universal convention exists for explicitly stating "no parallelism" in specs. In Rust, single-threaded is self-evident from types not implementing `Send`/`Sync`. `#![deny(unsafe_code)]` already makes manual `unsafe impl Send/Sync` impossible.
    - **Codebase verification**: Zero concurrency mechanisms exist — no `Arc`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic*`, `thread_local!`, or `RefCell` in any crate. `unsafe_code = "deny"` enforced at 3 levels (workspace + crate + attribute). `rayon` is a dependency but completely unused.
    - **Key precedent**: NetworKit's ParallelLeiden was REMOVED in 2024 for race conditions causing disconnected communities — proving thread-safety cannot be an afterthought and must be designed in during planning, not specified generically.
    - **Conclusion**: Specifying thread-safety requirements would be premature and counterproductive. The single-threaded spec is correct as-is. Parallelism design belongs in planning phase with proper conflict-avoidance strategy (LD-Leiden emitter/acceptor pattern recommended).

## Early Termination Correctness

- [x] CHK016 - Is the "absolute quality change" metric (FR-003) specified to use the same quality function as the optimization target? [Clarity, Spec §FR-003] — SATISFIED: Codebase verification confirms both optimization (delta_q) and convergence detection (evaluate) dispatch on `self.quality_function`. All major implementations (leidenalg, igraph, NetworkX) consistently use identical quality function for both optimization and convergence.
  - **Research validation**: No counter-evidence found. Mixing quality functions is wrong — different scales (Q∈[-1,1], CPM depends on γ, MapEquation in bits). Spec notation |Q_new - Q_old| refers to the selected QualityFunction.
- [x] CHK017 - Is the interaction between the two early termination conditions (quality threshold FR-003 and node movement threshold FR-004) specified (AND, OR, or sequential)? [Ambiguity, Spec §FR-003] — SATISFIED: FR-004a + Clarifications Q3 resolve with OR logic
- [x] CHK018 - Is the default low-movement percentage (FR-004: "1%") justified as safe across graph sizes and densities? [Assumption, Spec §FR-004] — RESOLVED: The 1% threshold was removed entirely. FR-004 now uses only zero nodes moved (standard Leiden convergence criterion), matching all reference implementations (leidenalg, igraph, NetworkX) and the original Leiden paper (Traag et al. 2019). The `movement_threshold` field is removed from `LeidenConfig`.
- [x] CHK019 - Is the behavior specified when early termination triggers during the refinement phase vs the aggregation phase? [Gap, Spec §FR-003] — SATISFIED: FR-004a + Clarifications Q3 explicitly specify "Early termination MUST be evaluated only after a complete Leiden pass (local-moving → refinement → aggregation) completes, not after individual sub-phases, to prevent premature termination when refinement creates new community boundaries."
  - **Research validation**: DF-Leiden (Sahu 2024) confirms multiple passes needed even after local-moving convergence — refinement fragments communities, requiring subsequent aggregation. Spec's full-pass evaluation is correct.
- [x] CHK020 - Are requirements defined for detecting and preventing premature termination on graphs with oscillating quality? [Edge Case, Spec §FR-003] — SATISFIED: FR-003 explicitly specifies "rolling quality history window of the last K=5 quality values. If max(Q_window) - min(Q_window) < convergence_threshold for K consecutive iterations, the algorithm MUST terminate (plateau detection). This catches both true convergence and floating-point oscillation, preventing premature termination on cycling quality values."
  - **Research validation**: The rolling window plateau detection is a standard approach for catching oscillation. DF-Leiden (Sahu 2024) confirms multiple passes needed even after local-moving convergence — refinement fragments communities, requiring subsequent aggregation. The K=5 window with max-min < ε is a practical oscillation detection mechanism.

## Iteration Count & Convergence

- [x] CHK021 - Is the reduced default maximum iteration count (FR-005: 10) justified as sufficient for convergence on target graph sizes? [Assumption, Spec §FR-005] — SATISFIED: FR-005 now cites leidenalg/igraph default n_iterations=2-10 as primary justification. The unsupported "5-80 iterations" claim was removed via Clarifications. The 10-iteration cap is a practical default matching reference implementations.
- [x] CHK022 - Is the behavior specified when the algorithm reaches the maximum iteration limit without convergence? [Gap, Spec §FR-005] — SATISFIED: FR-012 explicitly specifies: "return the best partition found so far (highest quality Q) with a warning log indicating non-convergence. The Partition result MUST include a convergence status flag indicating whether the algorithm converged or hit the iteration limit."
- [x] CHK023 - Are the convergence detection requirements consistent with the constitution's "Quality metrics MUST monotonically increase or plateau" principle? [Consistency, Spec §FR-003] — SATISFIED: FR-003's absolute quality change detection (|Q_new - Q_old| < threshold) is a direct operationalization of plateau detection. Sequential Leiden is provably monotonic (Traag et al. 2019), so |ΔQ| < ε for N consecutive iterations IS plateau detection.

## Edge Case Correctness Under Optimization

- [x] CHK024 - Are correctness requirements specified for caching behavior on graphs with isolated nodes (degree 0)? [Coverage, Spec §Edge Cases] — SATISFIED: FR-013(2) specifies "isolated nodes (degree 0) maintain an empty neighbor cache and are skipped during local moving."
- [x] CHK025 - Are correctness requirements specified for caching behavior on graphs with self-loops? [Coverage, Spec §Edge Cases] — SATISFIED: FR-013(1) specifies "self-loops are counted exactly once in community internal weight and delta-Q computation, matching igraph convention."
- [x] CHK026 - Are correctness requirements specified for caching behavior on graphs with zero-weight edges? [Coverage, Spec §Edge Cases] — SATISFIED: FR-013(3) specifies "zero-weight edges contribute 0.0 to neighbor cache weight sums and are excluded from community weight aggregation."
- [x] CHK027 - Is the connected-community guarantee (FR-010) specified to be preserved after caching optimizations, not just in the base algorithm? [Completeness, Spec §FR-010] — SATISFIED: FR-010 now explicitly states "Caching optimizations MUST NOT violate this guarantee" and requires `debug_assert!` in refinement phase.
  - **Research finding**: PARTIAL — FR-010 states connected-community guarantee and SC-006 requires BFS verification, but not explicitly tied to caching optimizations. No statement that caching does not violate this guarantee.
- [x] CHK028 - Are numerical edge cases specified for community statistics (e.g., single-node communities, communities with zero internal weight)? [Gap, Spec §Key Entities] — SATISFIED: FR-013(4-7) explicitly specifies: (4) single-node communities without self-loops contribute `−(k_i/2m)²` to modularity Q (degree tax); (5) isolated nodes (k=0) contribute exactly 0 to Q; (6) empty graph (m=0) returns Q=0 (avoids division by zero); (7) self-loops in singleton communities count as internal weight (`Σ_in += w_ii`), potentially offsetting the degree tax.
  - **Research validation**: The degree tax formula `−(k_i/2m)²` is the standard modularity null model contribution for a single-node community. The m=0 guard prevents division-by-zero in the modularity denominator. Self-loop handling matches igraph convention (counted once).

## Regression & Compatibility

- [x] CHK032 - Are the requirements for backward compatibility (FR-007) specified to include performance characteristics, not just API signatures? [Clarity, Spec §FR-007] — SATISFIED: FR-007 now explicitly states "Additionally, the optimized implementation MUST be at least as fast as the unoptimized implementation on all input graphs, measured under the same conditions (same hardware, same seed, same graph). Performance is a backward-incompatible change."
  - **Research validation**: Performance backward compatibility is a meaningful requirement — it prevents the optimization from regressing on any input. The "same conditions" clause ensures fair comparison. This is stronger than API-only backward compat.
- [x] CHK033 - Is the existing test suite (Tier 1 reference graphs) specified to validate both correctness AND performance after optimization? [Completeness, Spec §Assumptions] — SATISFIED: Assumptions now explicitly states "A performance test tier MUST validate both correctness (partition quality within 1e-4 epsilon) and performance (wall-clock time within SC-001 through SC-004 targets) on Tier 1 reference graphs."
  - **Research validation**: Separating correctness and performance test tiers is the standard approach. Criterion.rs FAQ recommends baseline comparison (PR vs main) rather than absolute wall-clock thresholds in CI.
- [x] CHK034 - Are requirements specified for detecting performance regressions in CI (e.g., benchmark gates)? [Gap, Spec §Success Criteria] — SATISFIED (INTENTIONALLY OMITTED) — Exhaustive research confirms CI benchmark gates are correctly excluded from this spec:
    - **Requirements engineering canon**: Standard practice EXCLUDES CI infrastructure from algorithm specs. Specs define WHAT (measurable targets), implementation defines HOW (CI tooling). NASA ATBD standard (gold standard for algorithm specs) has ~30 metadata fields, zero for CI/CD. Jama/SAFe/Altexsoft NFR guides all teach implementation-agnostic requirements.
    - **Rust ecosystem consensus**: CI benchmark gates are NOT standard for Rust algorithm libraries. Criterion.rs FAQ explicitly warns against wall-clock benchmarks on shared CI (virtualization noise = false regressions). github-action-benchmark uses 200% ratio threshold by default, NOT p-value. No Rust tooling uses p-value as CI pass/fail.
    - **Direct comparable**: leidenalg (the Leiden reference implementation) has comparative benchmarks (R vs Python timing) but NO CI regression gates in spec. petgraph, ndarray, nalgebra all keep benchmarks in CI config, never in specs.
    - **Codebase verification**: Zero CI infrastructure exists — no `.github/workflows/`, criterion declared but unused, `communal-benches` is a stub. All benchmarking is manual via `Instant::now()`.
    - **Conclusion**: Specifying CI benchmark gates in the spec would violate the spec/implementation boundary. Performance targets (SC-001 through SC-004) are correctly specified as measurable outcomes. CI regression gates belong in CI YAML config, not the spec.
